title: The divine senses and the opened heavens
source_text: Εἰ καὶ μὴ ἀπολογήσεται οὖν ὁ Ἰουδαῖος περὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ Ἡσαΐου, κοινοποιούντων ἡμῶν τὰ περὶ τῆς ἀνοίξεως τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐπὶ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀκουσθείσης αὐτῷ φωνῆς καὶ τὰ ὅμοια εὑρισκόντων ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ ἀναγεγραμμένα καὶ ἐν τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ ἢ καί τινι ἄλλῳ προφήτῃ. ἡμεῖς γε τὸν λόγον ὅση δύναμις ἡμῖν παραστήσομεν λέγοντες ὅτι, ὥσπερ ὄναρ πεπίστευται πολλοὺς πεφαντασι ῶσθαι τινὰ μὲν θειότερα τινὰ δὲ περὶ μελλόντων βιωτικῶν ἀναγγέλλοντα εἴτε σαφῶς εἴτε καὶ δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων, καὶ τοῦτ᾿ ἐναργές ἐστι παρὰ πᾶσι τοῖς παραδεξαμένοις πρόνοιαν, οὕτως τί ἄτοπον τὸ τυποῦν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἐν ὀνείρῳ δύνασθαι αὐτὸ τυποῦν καὶ ὕπαρ πρὸς τὸ χρήσιμον τῷ ἐν ᾧ τυποῦται ἢ τοῖς παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἀκουσομένοις; καὶ ὥσπερ φαντασίαν λαμβάνομεν ὄναρ ἀκούειν καὶ πλήσσεσθαι τὴν αἰσθητὴν ἀκοὴν καὶ ὁρᾶν δι᾿ ὀφθαλμῶν, οὔτε τῶν τοῦ σώματος ὀφθαλμῶν οὔτε τῆς ἀκοῆς πλησσομένης ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ ταῦτα πάσχοντος, οὕτως οὐδὲν ἄτοπον τοιαῦτα γεγονέναι ἐπὶ τῶν προφητῶν, ὅτε ἀναγέγραπται ἑωρακέναι τινὰ αὐτοὺς παραδοξότερα ἢ ἀκηκοέναι λόγους κυρίου ἢ τεθεωρηκέναι οὐρανοὺς ἀνοιγομένους. ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐχ ὑπολαμβάνω τὸν αἰσθητὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῷχθαι καὶ τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀνοιγνύμενον διῃρῆσθαι, ἵνα ἀναγράψῃ τὸ τοιοῦτον Ἰεζεκιήλ. μή ποτ᾿ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος τὸν φρονίμως ἀκούοντα τῶν εὐαγγελίων τὸ ὅμοιον ἐκδεκτέον, κἂν προσκόπτῃ τὸ τοιοῦτον τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις, οἳ διὰ πολλὴν ἁπλότητα κινοῦσι τὸν κόσμον, σχίζοντες τὸ τηλικοῦτον σῶμα ἡνωμένον τοῦ παντὸς οὐρανοῦ. ὁ δὲ βαθύτερον τὸ τοιοῦτον ἐξετάζων ἐρεῖ ὅτι οὔσης, ὡς ἡ γραφὴ ὠνόμασε, θείας τινὸς γενικῆς αἰσθήσεως, ἣν μόνος ὁ μακάριος εὑρίσκει ἤδη κατὰ τὸ λεγόμενον καὶ παρὰ τῷ Σολομῶντι· „ὅτι αἴσθησιν θείαν εὑρήσεις,“ καὶ ὄντων εἰδῶν ταύτης τῆς αἰσθήσεως, ὁράσεως πεφυκυίας βλέπειν τὰ κρείττονα σωμάτων πράγματα, ἐν οἷς δηλοῦται τὰ χερουβὶμ ἢ τὰ σεραφὶμ, καὶ ἀκοῆς ἀντιληπτικῆς φωνῶν οὐχὶ ἐν ἀέρι τὴν οὐσίαν ἐχουσῶν, καὶ γεύσεως χρωμένης ἄρτῳ ζῶντι καὶ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβεβηκότι καὶ ζωὴν διδόντι τῷ κόσμῳ, οὕτω δὲ καὶ ὀσφρήσεως ὀσφραινομένης τοιῶνδε, καθὸ „Χριστοῦ εὐωδία“ λέγει εἶναι „τῷ θεῷ“ Παῦλος, καὶ ἁφῆς, καθ᾿ ἣν Ἰωάννης φησὶ ταῖς χερσὶν ἐψηλαφηκέναι „περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς“· οἱ μακάριοι προφῆται τὴν θείαν αἴσθησιν εὑρόντες καὶ βλέποντες θείως καὶ ἀκούοντες θείως καὶ γευόμενοι ὁμοίως καὶ ὀσφραινόμενοι, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, αἰσθήσει οὐκ αἰσθητῇ καὶ ἁπτόμενοι τοῦ λόγου μετὰ πίστεως, ὥστ᾿ ἀποῤῥοὴν αὐτοῦ ἥκειν εἰς αὐτοὺς θεραπεύσουσαν αὐτοὺς, οὕτως ἑώρων ἃ ἀναγράφουσιν ἑωρακέναι καὶ ἤκουον ἃ λέγουσιν ἀκηκοέναι καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια ἔπασχον, ὡς ἀνέγραφον, ἐσθίοντες „κεφαλίδα“ διδομένην αὐτοῖς βιβλίου. οὕτω δὲ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ „ὠσφράνθη τῆς ὀσμῆς τῶν“ τοῦ υἱοῦ θειοτέρων „ἱματίων“ καὶ ἐπεῖπε πνευματικῇ εὐλογίᾳ τό· „ἰδοὺ ὀσμὴ τοῦ υἱοῦ μου ὡς ὀσμὴ ἀγροῦ πλήρους, ὃν εὐλόγησεν ὁ κύριος.“ παραπλησίως δὲ τούτοις καὶ νοητῶς μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθητῶς Ἰησοῦς „ηψατο“ τοῦ λεπροῦ, ἵν᾿ αὐτὸν καθαρίσῃ, ὡς ἐγὼ οἶμαι, διχῶς, ἀπαλλάττων αὐτὸν οὐ μόνον, ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ ἀκούουσι, λέπρας αἰσθητῆς δι᾿ αἰσθητῆς ἁφῆς ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἄλλης διὰ τῆς ὡς ἀληθῶς θείας αὐτοῦ ἁφῆς, οὕτως οὖν „ἐμαρτύρησεν Ἰωάννης λέγων ὅτι τεθέαμαι τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον ὡς περιστερὰν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν. κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ πέμψας με βαπτίζειν ἐν τῷ ὕδατι, ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν· ἐφ᾿ ὃν ἂν ἴδῃς τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον καὶ μένον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ βαπτίζων ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, κἀγὼ ἑώρακα, καὶ μεμαρτύρηκα ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.“ καὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ γε ἠνοίχθησαν οἱ οὐρανοί· καὶ τότε μὲν πλὴν Ἰωάννου οὐδεὶς ἀναγέγραπται ἑωρακέναι ἀνοιχθέντας τοὺς οὐρανούς. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἀνοιχθῆναι τοὺς οὐρανοὺς προλέγων τοῖς μαθηταῖς ὁ σωτὴρ ἐσόμενον ὀψομένοις αὐτό φησιν· „ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.“ καὶ οὕτως Παῦλος ἡρπάγη εἰς τρίτον οὐρανὸν, πρότερον ἰδὼν αὐτὸν ἀνοιχθέντα, ἐπεὶ μαθητὴς ἦν Ἰησοῦ. διηγήσασθαι δὲ νῦν, διὰ τί ὁ Παῦλος λέγει τό· „εἴτε ἐν σώματι οὐκ οἶδα, εἴτε ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος οὐκ οἶδα, ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν,“ οὐ τοῦ παρόντος ἐστὶ καιροῦ. ἔτι δὲ προσθήσω τῷ λόγῳ καὶ αὐτὰ, ἃ οἴεται ὁ Κέλσος, ὅτι αὐτὸς Ἰησοῦς εἶπε τὰ περὶ τὴν ἄνοιξιν τῶν οὐρανῶν καὶ τὸ καταβὰν πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν (ἐν) εἴδει περιστερᾶς παρὰ τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ· τῆς γραφῆς τοῦτο οὐ παραστησάσης, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἶπε τοῦτο ἑωρακέναι. οὐ συνεῖδε δ᾿ ὁ γενναιότατος ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι κατὰ τὸν εἰπόντα τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐπὶ τῇ ἐν τῷ ὄρει ὀπτασίᾳ· „μηδενὶ εἴπητε τὸ ὅραμα, ἕως ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ,“ εἰρηκέναι τοῖς μαθηταῖς τὸ παρὰ τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ὀφθὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰωάννου καὶ ἀκουσθέν, ἐνιδεῖν δὲ ἔστι καὶ τῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἤθει πανταχοῦ περιϊσταμένου τὴν περιαυτολογίαν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο λέγοντος „κἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής.“ καὶ ἐπὶ περιΐστατο τὴν περιαυτολογίαν καὶ τοῖς ἔργοις μᾶλλον ἐβούλετο δηλοῦν εἶναι Χριστὸς ἤπερ τῇ λέξει, διὰ τοῦτό φασιν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι πρὸς αὐτόν· „εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς, εἰπὲ ἡμῖν παῤῥησίᾳ.“ ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἰουδαῖός ἐστιν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ λέγων τῷ Ἰησοῦ περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐν εἴδει περιστρᾶς τό· πλὴν ὅτι σὺ φῂς καί τινα ἕνα ἐπάγῃ τῶν μετὰ σοῦ κεκολασμένων, ἀναγκαῖον αὐτῷ παραστῆσαι ὅτι καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ οἰκείως τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ προσώπῳ περιέθηκεν. οὐδὲ γὰρ συνάπτουσι τὸν Ἰωάννην οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν Ἰωάννου τῇ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κολάσει. καὶ ἐν τούτῳ οὖν ἐλέγχεται ὁ πάντ᾿ ἀλαζονευσάμενος εἰδέναι μὴ ἐγνωκὼς, τίνα προσάψῃ ῥήματα τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν προσώπῳ.
pass_a_gloss: Even if then the Jew will not make a defence (ἀπολογέομαι) about Ezekiel and Isaiah, we making common/comparing (κοινοποιέω) the things about the opening (ἄνοιξις) of the heavens at Jesus and the voice heard by him, and finding the like things recorded in Ezekiel and in Isaiah or some other prophet, we at least will establish (παρίστημι) the argument as far as power is ours, saying that, just as it is believed that many in dream (ὄναρ) have had impressions presented (φαντασιόομαι), some more divine (θειότερα), some announcing (ἀναγγέλλω) future things of life (βιωτικά), whether clearly (σαφῶς) or through riddles (αἰνίγματα), and this is evident (ἐναργές) to all who accept providence (πρόνοια), so what is absurd (ἄτοπον) that what imprints (τυπόω) the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) in a dream be able to imprint it also awake (ὕπαρ) for the benefit of the one in whom it is imprinted or of those who will hear from him? And just as we receive an impression (φαντασία) in dream of hearing and of the sense-hearing (αἰσθητὴ ἀκοή) being struck (πλήσσω) and of seeing through eyes, neither the eyes of the body nor the hearing being struck but the ruling part suffering (πάσχω) these things, so nothing absurd that such things happened to the prophets, when it is recorded they saw certain more marvellous things or heard words of the Lord (λόγοι κυρίου) or beheld (θεωρέω) heavens being opened. For I do not suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) the perceptible heaven (αἰσθητὸς οὐρανός) was opened and its body, being opened, divided (διαιρέω), so that Ezekiel might record such a thing. Perhaps then (μή ποτ᾿ οὖν) also in the case of the Saviour (σωτήρ) the one hearing the gospels prudently (φρονίμως) must understand (ἐκδεκτέον) the like, even if such stumbles (προσκόπτω) the simpler (ἁπλούστεροι), who through much simplicity (ἁπλότης) move the cosmos (κινοῦσι τὸν κόσμον), splitting (σχίζω) so great a united (ἡνωμένον) body of the whole heaven. But the one examining more deeply (βαθύτερον ἐξετάζω) will say that — there being, as Scripture named it, a certain divine generic sense (θεία τις γενικὴ αἴσθησις), which only the blessed one (ὁ μακάριος) finds already, according to what is said also in Solomon, 'that you will find divine sense (αἴσθησιν θείαν εὑρήσεις)', and there being species (εἴδη) of this sense: of sight (ὅρασις) naturally fit to see things better than bodies, in which the cherubim or seraphim are shown; of hearing (ἀκοή) apprehending (ἀντιληπτική) voices not having their being (οὐσία) in air; and of taste (γεῦσις) using living bread (ἄρτος ζῶν) both come down from heaven and giving life to the world; so also of smell (ὄσφρησις) smelling such things, according to which Paul says he is 'a fragrance (εὐωδία) of Christ to God'; and of touch (ἁφή), according to which John says he handled (ψηλαφάω) with hands 'concerning the Word of life (λόγος τῆς ζωῆς)' — the blessed prophets, having found the divine sense, and seeing divinely (θείως) and hearing divinely and tasting likewise and smelling, so to name it, by a sense not sensible (αἰσθήσει οὐκ αἰσθητῇ), and touching the Word with faith (πίστις), so that an emanation (ἀπορροή) of him came to them going to heal (θεραπεύω) them, thus saw what they record they saw and heard what they say they heard and suffered the like things, as they recorded, eating a 'roll (κεφαλίς)' of a book given to them. So also Isaac 'smelled the smell of the' more divine 'garments (ἱμάτια)' of his son and said over (ἐπεῖπε) in spiritual blessing (πνευματικὴ εὐλογία): 'Behold the smell of my son as the smell of a full field which the Lord blessed.' Similarly to these and intelligibly (νοητῶς) rather than sensibly (αἰσθητῶς) Jesus 'touched' the leper, that he might cleanse (καθαρίζω) him, as I think, doubly (διχῶς), freeing (ἀπαλλάττω) him not only, as the many hear, from sensible leprosy (λέπρα) through sensible touch, but also from the other through his truly divine touch. Thus then 'John witnessed saying, I have beheld (θεάομαι) the Spirit descending as a dove from heaven, and it remained (μένω) on him. And I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water, that one said to me: On whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him, this is the one baptizing in Holy Spirit; and I have seen and have witnessed that this is the Son of God (υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ).' And to Jesus the heavens were opened; and then, except John, no one is recorded to have seen the heavens opened. This opening of the heavens the Saviour, foretelling (προλέγω) to the disciples that it would be, they being about to see it, says: 'Amen amen I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.' And so Paul was snatched (ἁρπάζω) to a third heaven, having first seen it opened, since he was a disciple of Jesus. To narrate now why Paul says: 'whether in body I do not know, whether outside the body I do not know, God knows,' is not of the present occasion (καιρός). Further I will add to the argument also the very things which Celsus thinks, that Jesus himself told the things about the opening of the heavens and the Holy Spirit come down on him in dove-form at the Jordan, Scripture not presenting this, that he himself said he saw it. The most noble one (ὁ γενναιότατος, ironic) did not perceive (συνοράω) that it is not in keeping with the one who said to the disciples at the vision (ὀπτασία) on the mountain, 'Tell no one the vision (ὅραμα) until the Son of Man rises from the dead,' to have told the disciples what was seen and heard by John at the Jordan; and one may see it in the character (ἦθος) of Jesus, everywhere avoiding (περιίσταμαι) self-praise/talk about himself (περιαυτολογία), and therefore saying, 'Even if I say about myself, my testimony (μαρτυρία) is not true.' And since he avoided talk of himself and wished to show by deeds (ἔργα) rather than by speech (λέξις) that he was Christ, therefore the Jews say to him, 'If you are the Christ, tell us openly (παρρησίᾳ).' And since it is a Jew in Celsus saying to Jesus, about the things of the Holy Spirit in dove-form: 'except that you say, and bring in (ἐπάγω) some one of those punished (κολάζω) with you,' it is necessary to show him that this too he did not fittingly (οἰκείως) attach (περιτίθημι) to the Jewish character (πρόσωπον). For the Jews do not join (συνάπτω) John to Jesus, and John's punishment to Jesus' punishment (κόλασις). And in this then he is refuted (ἐλέγχω) who boasted (ἀλαζονεύομαι) to know everything, not having known what words (ῥήματα) to attach to the Jewish character addressing Jesus.
pass_b_english: Even if the Jew, then, will not make a defence for Ezekiel and Isaiah when we place side by side the opening of the heavens for Jesus, with the voice he heard, and the like things we find recorded in Ezekiel and in Isaiah (Ezekiel 1:1; Isaiah 6:1–2) or in some other prophet, we at least will support our case as best we can. We say that, just as it is believed that many have had visions in dreams, some of more divine things, others telling of future events of this life, whether clearly or in riddles, and this is plain to all who accept providence, so what is absurd in holding that what forms impressions on the ruling mind in a dream can form them on it while awake as well, for the benefit of the one in whom they are formed, or of those who will hear of them from him? And just as in a dream we have the impression that we hear and that our bodily ear is struck, and that we see with our eyes, though neither the eyes of the body nor the hearing is being struck, but the ruling mind is undergoing these things, so there is nothing absurd in such things having happened to the prophets, when it is recorded that they saw certain quite extraordinary things, or heard words of the Lord, or beheld the heavens opening. For I do not suppose that the visible heaven was opened, and its body split apart as it opened, so that Ezekiel might record such a thing.

Perhaps, then, in the case of the Saviour too, whoever listens to the Gospels with understanding should take it in the same way, even if such a view offends the simpler sort, who in their great simplicity set the universe moving, splitting the vast, unified body of the whole heaven. But one who examines the matter more deeply will say this. There is, as Scripture has named it, a divine sense, general in kind, which only the blessed man finds even now, according to what is said in Solomon too: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5). This sense has its kinds: a sight naturally able to see things higher than bodies, among which the cherubim or the seraphim are shown (Ezekiel 10:1; Isaiah 6:2); a hearing that receives voices whose being is not in the air; a taste that feeds on living bread, which has come down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33, 51); so too a smell that smells such things as Paul means when he speaks of being “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15); and a touch, by which John says he has handled with his hands “the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). The blessed prophets found this divine sense. They saw in a divine way and heard in a divine way, and tasted and smelled in the same way, by a sense that, if I may so name it, is not of the senses; and they touched the Word with faith, so that an outflow from him came to them to heal them. In this way they saw what they record that they saw, and heard what they say they heard, and had the like experiences as they wrote of them, eating the “roll” of a book that was given to them (Ezekiel 2:9–3:3).

So too Isaac “smelled the smell of” his son's more divine “garments,” and spoke these words as a spiritual blessing: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). In a like way, Jesus “touched” the leper (Matthew 8:3) with a touch of the mind rather than of the senses, to cleanse him, as I think, in two ways: he freed him not only, as most people take it, from bodily leprosy by a bodily touch, but also from the other leprosy by his truly divine touch.

It was in this way, then, that “John bore witness, saying: ‘I have seen the Spirit descending as a dove from heaven, and it remained on him. And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, “He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And I have seen, and have borne witness that this is the Son of God’” (John 1:32–34). And for Jesus the heavens were opened (Matthew 3:16), and at that time no one but John is recorded to have seen the heavens opened. But the Saviour, foretelling to his disciples that this opening of the heavens would come, and that they would see it, says: “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). And so Paul was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), having first seen it opened, since he was a disciple of Jesus. But to explain now why Paul says, “Whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12:2), does not belong to the present occasion.

Further, I will add to my argument the very point Celsus assumes: that Jesus himself told of the opening of the heavens and of the Holy Spirit that came down upon him in the form of a dove at the Jordan, although Scripture does not present him as saying that he saw this. This most noble man did not see that it does not fit the one who said to his disciples about the vision on the mountain, “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matthew 17:9), to have told his disciples what John saw and heard at the Jordan. One may see this also in the character of Jesus, who everywhere avoided speaking about himself and for that reason said, “Even if I speak about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And since he avoided speaking about himself, and wished to show that he was the Christ by his deeds rather than by his words, for this reason the Jews say to him, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).

But since it is a Jew in Celsus who says to Jesus, about the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, “Except that you say so, and bring forward one of those who were punished with you,” we must show Celsus that this too he has not fittingly attributed to the Jewish character. For the Jews do not link John with Jesus, nor John's punishment with the punishment of Jesus. In this too, then, the man who boasted that he knew everything stands convicted, for he did not know what words to give the Jewish character in addressing Jesus.

choices.choice: Ezekiel 1:1 and Isaiah 6:1–2 are the two visions Origen quoted in 1.43; Isaiah does not speak of opened heavens, but Origen sets his throne vision beside Ezekiel's. Proverbs 2:5: Origen reads αἴσθησιν θείαν εὑρήσεις ('you will find a divine sense'), as he does elsewhere; the common LXX text has ἐπίγνωσιν θεοῦ εὑρήσεις ('knowledge of God'); cited as Proverbs 2:5 on Origen's own attribution. 'Only the blessed man finds' may echo Proverbs 3:13 ('blessed is the man who has found wisdom'); possible only, not cited inline. Cherubim and seraphim: Ezekiel 10:1 and Isaiah 6:2. 1 John 1:1 has 'our hands handled ... concerning the Word of life'; the English drops the 'concerning' (περί) for readable order. 'Touching the Word with faith, so that an outflow from him came to heal them' may allude to the woman healed by touching Jesus (Mark 5:27–30; Luke 8:44–46); possible only, not cited inline. Ezekiel 2:9 LXX κεφαλὶς βιβλίου ('roll of a book'), eaten at 3:1–3. Genesis 27:27 LXX; 'more divine' and 'his son's' are Origen's insertions into the quotation. The leper's touch: Matthew 8:3 (also Mark 1:41; Luke 5:13). John 1:51 quoted without ἀπ᾿ ἄρτι. Matthew 17:9: Origen has ἀναστῇ as Mark 9:9, but τὸ ὅραμα is Matthew's word. John 5:31: Origen's wording κἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω differs from the Gospel's ἐὰν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ. 2 Corinthians 12:2 cited for both the third heaven and the 'in the body' words (repeated in 12:3). Celsus's quoted words are from 1.41.
